transcript: Going into the 1990s,   running a big beefy enterprise server  meant UNIX software on RISC hardware. Then came Intel. And upon its silicon horse rode  two powerful operating systems. One was Windows,   which everyone first thought would win the market. But then came this new, fast-moving thing   written with the contributions of  thousands around the world. Linux. In today's video, one of the most fascinating  industrial transitions in computer history:   How Intel, Microsoft and Linux  came together to take down UNIX. ## Beginnings It is the 1990s and Chipzilla is  seeking new worlds to conquer. They had won the consumer PC  world by masterfully leveraging   the PC's massive sales volumes. High  volume improves semiconductor yield. Better yield reduces costs, raises profits,  and throws off more cash to invest back into   better manufacturing. Intel grabbed a lead that  competitors like AMD and Cyrix cannot overcome. Intel believed that it can run the same playbook  in the world of enterprise servers. Such servers   are used by corporate clients to manage  and serve multiple “client” computers. Sometimes, people group servers together  with workstations - which are more powerful   desktop computers for intense tasks like  graphics or scientific applications. Such   workstations can also serve a file or two  over a LAN - acting as a low-end server. On the high end, there are big monolith  computers powered by many CPUs with support   for 64-bit and virtual machine as well as lots  of memory. They run databases, file storage,   and complex business applications -  providing beefy compute via network. They can also serve websites - which  later became a massive market as the   Internet craze expanded. Though you  don't need a high end machine for that. ## Vertically Integrated At the start of the decade, this enterprise server market was dominated  by vertically-integrated system vendors. Such vendors offered a closed, proprietary  system often based on RISC CPUs running a   variant of the UNIX operating system.  The largest and most famous vendor   was Sun Microsystem - which offered their  SPARC chips and Solaris operating system. Others included IBM with their POWER RISC  chips running the AIX operating system. And Hewlett-Packard, with their  PA-RISC chips running the HP-UX   operating system. Silicon Graphics as well. These systems were expensive - running into the  hundreds of thousands of dollars. What's more,   their proprietary nature made switching  nigh impossible. Buy in, get locked in. ## Windows NT But if Intel wanted to enter the server  market, it needed a strong software partner. And where did this bring them? To  Microsoft ... and Windows NT. Released   in 1993 by a team led by the legendary  Dave Cutler, NT is a proprietary OS for   both workstations and servers separate  from the consumer-oriented Windows. While Windows NT Server looks similar  to the consumer product and can run   the same applications, they were  quite different beneath the hood. Regular Windows is a graphical shell grotesquely  grafted on top of the MS-DOS operating system.   It is said to be possible to clip through  into the horrors of the Backrooms beyond. NT on the other hand was written from the  ground up for the enterprise. Microsoft   marketed it as being more powerful,  reliable, and with enhanced security. The first version of NT Server ran on  the Intel 386. It worked fine but it   didn't exactly set the world ablaze. NT was  immature, missing features and capabilities   that its competitors - like IBM's OS/2,  Novell's NetWare and the UNIX variants - had. And it required rather powerful hardware  (for the time): 16 megabytes of RAM. In 1993,   NT Server sold about 30,000 units  - undoubtedly a disappointment. But Microsoft is like the Terminator or sequels  to Air Bud: They just keep on coming. Redmond   stayed in the market - adding new features  and sending the UNIX vendors scrambling. In 1994, Microsoft sold about  115,000 NT licenses. An improvement,   though sales still lagged that of even its  Workstation sibling. But they were growing. ## Pentium Pro In late 1995, Intel presented  the first chip they really felt   could take them to the server  space: the 32-bit Pentium Pro. I mentioned the Pentium Pro before.   It had 5.5 million transistors and ran  at about 150-200 megahertz - a great   leap over the original Pentium's 3.1  million transistors and 60 megahertz. The Pentium Pro slightly outperformed the fastest   RISC chips in certain integer benchmarks.  Which took the community by surprise. While faster RISC chips like the MIPS R10000  quickly matched afterwards, the Pro reset   the perceived performance limits of what was  previously deemed a mere "desktop" architecture.   The Pentium Pro thusly gave Intel the performance  wedge it needed to invade the server world. Vendors found that it together with the next  major version of Windows NT - version 4.0,   released earlier that same year - produced  a ready-made server standard that can   match the performance of some RISC-based  integrated systems at a far lower price. In mid-1995 Intel started circulating example  boards of what they called "Standard High Volume   Servers". These are basic reference models that  partners can adopt to accelerate time-to-market. The first generation boards  can support 1-4 Pentium Pros,   1-2 gigabytes of working memory, and  hundreds of gigabytes of storage. Intel   said that these servers can handle  up to 2,000 transactions per second. During the release presentation in  November, Intel announced Pentium   Pro-powered computers ranging from a  $2,600 workstation to a $20,000 server. In 1996, sales of Windows NT 4.0  grew by 85% - reaching 27% market   share according to IDC. The  competition remained strong,   but Wintel was building up a strong base in  servers, like what they have done in consumer. ## Border Skirmishes However, Intel knew there were risks in  chaining its enterprise future to Microsoft. While on the whole Microsoft and Intel  cooperated to grow the PC ecosystem,   breakouts still happened. Most infamously, in  1995 Intel introduced a multimedia software   standard they called "native  signal processing" or NSP. NSP was Intel’s effort to offload some  demanding audio and video compute to the   CPU via software and APIs. Their thinking was  simple: Get people to buy faster processors. But Microsoft saw NSP as a "middleware" that  bypassed the OS and so stepped into Windows’ turf.   Microsoft executives made it extremely clear to  Intel that they had issues and publicly announced   that they will not support it. CEO Bill Gates sent  an email to Andy Grove to express his irritation. The NSP Affair was not the only border  skirmish to occur during this time,   but it is the most well known. Mostly  because it came out during Microsoft's   anti-trust lawsuit as an example  of its anti-competitive behavior. And when it came out, the  two parties pooh-poohed it,   emphasizing that everything was alright.  But NSP reminded Intel that their partner   was more than willing to exercise its  leverage to kill things it didn’t like. Unlike the consumer versions of Windows, Windows  NT was built from the ground-up to be portable.   While most instances of NT ran on x86, it also  works on other hardwares like DEC's Alpha CPU,   IBM and Apple's PowerPC, and the RISC design MIPS. Microsoft continued to seal more chip  support deals - skillfully flanking   Intel right in front of it. A thought  emerged. If NT corners the market,   can Microsoft turn x86 and Intel into just  another hardware architecture amongst many? ## Mismatches Even if that does not happen, there  still remained the performance issues. With Moore's Law, Intel gets a new,  faster, better chip every two years.   But Microsoft puts out a new Windows  roughly every three to five years.   And that Windows doesn't always use  everything that Intel's chips had to offer. Most infamously, Intel first released a  32-bit chip in 1985 - the 386 processor.   Microsoft didn't bring out a 32-bit  consumer OS until 1995 - Windows 95,   in case you were wondering. Ten years later! Another one occurred during the  Pentium Pro development process,   recounted by Bob Colwell in his  book the Pentium Chronicles. Microsoft told Intel in many meetings that  Windows 95 (then known as "Chicago") was   going to be 32-bit only with all the  legacy 16-bit code to be removed. This   gave Intel the assurance to optimize  Pentium Pro for 32-bit performance. So imagine how much constructive confrontation was  forthcoming when Microsoft publicly announced in   1994 that Chicago's graphics display interface  - a key piece of the OS - will remain 16-bits. It was too late in the development cycle  for Intel to change the Pentium Pro,   so the show went on. And then when it came out,  Intel got dinged in the press for the chip’s   subpar graphics performance on consumer  desktops. Fortunately not a dealbreaker. And specifically regarding NT and the  server world, Intel felt that NT 4.0's   limits of 4-8 processors per OS instance  imposed a performance ceiling that kept it   out of the high end. To compare, some UNIX  variants can handle up to 64 processors. This mismatch ties back to the two’s different  growth models, Intel's growth depends on them   selling people the newest chip. So  they want software that helps do that. Microsoft on the other hand prioritizes  servicing their whole install base. So   they are going to take it slow - emphasizing  backwards compatibility and the whole ecosystem. And it is not like they don't invest -  developing a new Windows involves thousands   of employees and might cost billions  of dollars. It's just how software is. So Intel and Microsoft suffer that tension.  But what choice does Intel have with regards to   alternatives? In the late 1990s, one very strong  new candidate appeared on their radar: Linux. # Stallman In January 1984, a programmer at MIT named Richard  Stallman formally began a project to replace UNIX. Stallman hailed from the MIT AI Lab,   which appeared in my video about Lisp  machines, AI, and expert systems. Lisp began as an elegant research  tool for early AI research. But when   businesspeople recognized that Lisp and  the AI it powers can be a big industry,   the Lab split apart into two companies,  Symbolics and Lisp Machines Inc. Symbolics raised millions to try and  become the Nvidia of its day - hiring   away the Lab's top hackers and leaving it a  shell of itself. Stallman never forgave this.   "Everything's dying" he would later say. Motivated by deep feelings of  loss over his hacker community,   he decided to start a new one - founded  on top of the concept of free software. Thusly in late 1983, he embarked on  a project to build a free operating   system that followed UNIX's design  principles - like its modularity and   portability across hardware - without  copying it for trade secret reasons. The thing was called GNU - which he said  to mean "GNU's Not UNIX". Stallman didn't   know if he would ever finish it, but with such  things you will never know if you don’t start. Over the next few years, Stallman and his new  community built out the various bits of the   toolchain. But there was one thing missing:  The kernel, which suffered incessant delays. This was a pretty major piece. The  kernel bridges the OS and the hardware.   It manages memory, how much CPU  time a process gets, disk space,   and more. Even the name sounds important. It sits  at the very heart of the whole operating system. ## Linus and Linux That kernel finally arrived thanks to the  work of a 21-year old Finnish undergraduate   named Linus Torvalds, who was inspired by  an educational UNIX-based OS called MINIX. Very famous story. You probably  heard it before. In August 1991,   he posted on the MINIX Usenet group that he was  making a free hobbyist OS and requested feature   ideas. It drew contributors from that ecosystem  and eventually spun off into its own: Linux. Linus's role in the Linux project soon changes  from coder to that of a leader who reviews   other people’s contributions and merges them  into the code base. This approach - famously   described as like a bazaar - lets Linux  ship new code faster than companies can. The first workable version of Linux  released in October 1991. Then in 1992,   version 0.12 adopted Stallman's license, GPL.  This allowed anyone to read and modify Linux’s   code so long as those modifications  are also open sourced, if distributed. So GPL prevented companies from taking the code,   adding some salt on top and re-selling  the result as a competing closed-source   product - thereby saving the Linux kernel from  the same fragmentation issues that afflicted UNIX. It also assured companies that any work they did  to improve the kernel would help everyone and not   get locked away. Companies as large as IBM would  have hundreds of their employees contributing   code. Torvalds would later famously say that  going GPL was the best thing that he ever did. ## Distros and Red Hat The GPL also made possible the  business of commercial distribution. Linux is a kernel - a car engine. Very important,   but you still kinda need the rest of the  car. That might be fine for early adopters,   it is not practical to ask ordinary users  to build their car before driving it. So people started doing distributions  or "distros". Distributions package the   Linux kernel along with utilities from  the GNU Project or other free software   to produce an OS bundle that is  slightly more convenient to use. It is like those mixtapes we senior citizens  used to pass around to each other in high school. Good distros became popular enough to  monetize. Someone likened the business   model to selling bottled water. Different  packaging, same water ... unless you are   a Nongfu Water extremist and really into  the "natural over purified" water thing. Anyway. Notable early distributions of this  GNU/Linux operating system - which I must shorten   to Linux for the sake of brevity but let us not  forget GNU - include Slackware and Debian ... ... and Red Hat, which was first set up by  Marc Ewing in 1993. Ewing adopted Linux early,   but after some time realized that he was  spending more time managing his Linux   box than actually developing  software. I know the feeling. So he made a distribution called Red Hat in  the spare bedroom of his apartment near Duke   University. Named to memorialize a red  and white striped lacrosse cap he used   to wear in college. Though the logo looks  more like a fedora or a trilby, M’lady. Red Hat provided things around Linux  to make it a more professional product. Like for example, the Red Hat Package  Manager utility, which helps users add,   remove, or update software packages  that do stuff like Web or FTP. The Red Hat distribution can then be put  on a CD and sold in retail shops. In 1995,   Marc Ewing and colleague Robert Young founded Red  Hat the company, which earned revenue from selling   those CDs as well as accompanying training,  education and customer support services. In its first years, Linux was something  for highly technical hackers and broke   college students. The rise of Red Hat  and other commercial distributions like   Caldera helped usher Linux out of that early  space and into the corporate mainstream. ## An OS With Opportunity Linux adoption started small  but grew fast. By mid-1997,   its worldwide user base was conservatively  estimated at around 3-5 million. Yeah sure that far lags Windows' 100  million users and Apple Macintosh’s 50+   million. But in early 1992, Linux had maybe a  few hundred users. And 1996, maybe 1-2 million. What was driving all this uptake? It was more  than just price, though price of course played   a factor. A Red Hat disc and box retailed  at about $50. Windows NT licenses on the   other hand might sell for anywhere from $150  for a single upgrade to $1100 for a 10-seat   package. And UNIX systems with hardware and  software will cost $25,000 to $250,000 or more. Byte Magazine ran a story in 1997  mentioning a systems consultant for   Eastman Kodak installing Linux to aid in  some project for their Photo CD product,   and saving the company $10,000 by not  getting a high-priced UNIX alternative. Considering how the Photo CD  ended up, good savings indeed. But interestingly, companies and organizations  did not adopt Linux just because it was cheap.   A significant Linux advantage was  its reliability. One user said that   it was almost "crash-proof", which  translates to better productivity. And for sophisticated users, they loved that  they can access its source code - something   Microsoft would never let anyone do with  Windows. So people can customize their   Linux to do things on the fly. People  tweaked Linux to run on a Palm Pilot.   Researchers at Los Alamos used Linux to network  together 68 PCs to simulate atomic shock waves. On the other hand, it was true that Linux also  had glaring shortcomings. First and foremost,   it had nowhere near as many applications  as Windows or Mac. There was no good Linux   version of Microsoft Office, Visual  Basic, or other business software. I like how Byte said all that, then added right  afterwards that Linux did include lots of tools   that you can use to create your own applications.  That is the kind of audience, I reckon. Another issue is getting  support. If something goes wrong,   what documentation can you consult. And  who can you call? Though that is where   companies like Red Hat and Caldera  can step in, providing tech support. One last issue about Linux was its reputation.  Despite not sharing a direct lineage, it is   often associated with UNIX - which means receiving  UNIX's aura of being inscrutable and hard to use. And despite the fast growth, all  the prestigious names adopting it,   and the real price-performance benefits, there  still remained a negative bias amongst company   executives. A manager might often ask "How can  you possibly consider it for a critical server?" Yet even as they ask that, Linux probably was  already running somewhere in their company.   One anonymous system administrator  told the SF Chronicle in 1998: > "Many management types distrust Linux because  it is free. But they put me in charge of running   their servers and I am going to use what  works best. What works best is Linux". ## Meet Intel In early 1998, Intel started receiving these  strange requests from across the country. Engineers and researchers at places like US's   Fermi National Lab were asking Intel  to port its math libraries to Linux. Prior to this, Intel had minimal involvement  with Linux - maybe fixing a bug or two.   However, checks with OEMs making white-label  computer servers for customers like small   Internet Service Providers showed them  that Linux growth was exploding upwards. Almost 20% of public web servers ran it - an  unexpectedly high market share considering   that the OS had little to no presence on  the desktop. Still doesn't, by the way. This news went straight up to Andy Grove,  who remarked in rather colorful language   that they should be doing something about  this. So Intel executives reached out to   Red Hat and in a series of meetings, tried  to learn about how this company worked. And it sort of baffled them. Red Hat doesn't  own the underlying IP behind its core software   product, which anyone can get for free. How  does that make money? How’s this investable? But the guys at Red Hat kept talking. CEO  Robert Young liked to use this ketchup metaphor:   Anyone with tomatoes, sugar and vinegar can make  ketchup, yet Heinz owns 80% of that market. And   Linux advocates inside Intel shared data points  of what they learned on ISP adoption. In the end,   Intel management was convinced and the two  companies started talking about partnerships. As I mentioned earlier, Intel increasingly felt  that it would be risky to rely on just Windows NT.   They were working on a new chip called "Merced",  the first implementation of their 64-bit IA-64   server architecture. It shall later be branded  as Itanium, and was said to be blazingly fast. But worries lingered that NT would  shackle its full power - same as how   things went with 32-bit for literally a  decade. Perhaps reinforcing those fears,   Microsoft's next version of NT -  then called NT 5.0 - was delayed   from 1998 to 1999. After yet further delays,  Microsoft renamed NT 5.0 to Windows 2000. Now Intel can support and contribute to Linux  development - tuning it to take advantage   of Intel's latest and greatest silicon - and  make it a compelling alternative to Windows. ## Summer of Linux The summer of 1998 saw multiple big  companies making Linux announcements. In June 1998, IBM - one of the most  conservative companies out there - said   that it will include an open source web  server software called Apache in its suite   of e-commerce tools. Apache isn't Linux,  but most Apache server instances run on it. IBM first encountered Apache back in 1996  when they selected it for the website of   the Atlanta Summer Olympics. Now they  were giving it their stamp of approval,   officially giving open source its  first foothold into the enterprise. Another famous adopter was  Oracle. On July 6th 1998,   InfoWorld published an article titled  "Linux not yet critical mass". In it,   Oracle - plus Sybase and Informix - said  they had no intentions of releasing their   DB software for Linux. A rep said they weren’t  seeing a big demand from customers for it. Three days later, Oracle announced  that they were porting their Oracle8   database to Linux. A major reason  for this abrupt turnaround was a   panel discussion held at Santa Clara in  July 1998 called "the Future of Linux". Over 900 or so people came to see Torvalds  and others. In the panel, they discussed   whether open source was a fad, urged users to push  application vendors to port to Linux, and more. People later identify that panel as a major  turning point. By September 1998, several large   companies had Linux ports including the enterprise  systems company Computer Associates, software   maker Corel, and database company Informix. The  trend would continue in the subsequent years. ## Intel and Red Hat Intel was also at that July  "Future of Linux" panel. Intel's Sunil Saxena gave a presentation  saying that Linux was becoming the OS of   choice for Internet Service Providers while  also noting some of its weaknesses - like   scalability, drivers for high end  hardware, and large memory support. He emphasized that Intel wanted to support  Linux. And those words were soon backed with   action on September 29th when Intel announced  that it - along with the web browser company   Netscape and VC firms Benchmark and  Greylock - would invest in Red Hat. Now, Intel was saying they wanted Intel  silicon to run Linux as well as it did   Windows NT and everything else. They  will work with Red Hat - providing   technical contribution plus a dedicated Intel  engineering liaison for the Linux community. Cherry on top, Intel also said they  will join Linux International - an   early worldwide Linux advocacy organization. After the announcement, another  critical but underrated domino falls.   One Benchmark partner was also a board  member at Dell, and through him Red Hat   got in front of Michael Dell. They started  talking about Linux's growth on the server,   how the market might shape up, and  if Linux can ever win the desktop. Dell eventually invested into Red Hat. And  more importantly, they later announce in   early 1999 that they will start preinstalling  Linux on workstations and servers - the first   major vendor to do this. Suddenly Linux is  on the same pedestal as Windows and Novell. ## Microsoft When news of Intel's Red Hat investment  came out, the tech media went into a   frenzy speculating what this might mean  for the Intel-Microsoft relationship. Red Hat's executives recounted in  the book "Under the Radar" that   Microsoft "went ballistic" after Intel  announced their investment. That weekend,   Intel executives took multiple angry  calls from their Microsoft counterparts. Prior to 1998, Microsoft maybe could have nixed  the Intel investment. But in May that year,   the US government charged Microsoft  for monopolistic actions - particularly   regarding how it bundled Internet Explorer  with Windows during the Browser Wars. The trial and scrutiny meant that Microsoft had to   temper its behavior. Publicly they  issued a statement citing Red Hat as   evidence that Microsoft didn't actually  have a monopoly on operating systems. Interestingly, Microsoft would later  invoke Linux as evidence that there   remained enough competition in the OS market  that the government shouldn't break them up. But internally, they were  concerned. In October 1998,   a set of Microsoft memos - infamously  named the Halloween Memos - leaked,   called the rise of free software like Linux  a long-term credible threat to Windows. They then reportedly formed a "Linux  attack team" to convince customers   that it was not ready. They posted  a web page called "Linux Myths",   that tries to "step back from the  hype and look at the reality". It then addresses various "myths" chanted  by the Linux faithful like "Linux performs   better than Windows NT 4", and "Linux is more  reliable than Windows NT 4" and "Linux is free". Infamously in April 1999, Microsoft  sponsored benchmark tests by a third   party lab called Mindcraft that  showed NT outperforming Linux   as a file server by 2.5 times  and web server by 3.7 times. ## Port of Choice Intel dodged Gates’ fury by  declaring that it was OS neutral. So Linux, Novell’s Netware, Sun’s  Solaris and Microsoft’s Windows 2000,   Intel wanted all of them to  run well on its hardware. Intel (along with twenty other companies)  even tried to unite the thirty or so UNIX   variants out there using a thing  called Uniform Driver Initiative   so that vendors can write drivers for  Intel hardware. It didn't end up so well. Later in 2010, Intel would formalize this  Switzerland strategy as "Port of Choice",   but CTO Pat Gelsinger called it a long-standing  strategy in 2001. And in the end, the OS   makers had to accept it, because Intel  silicon then had no real alternatives. In mid-1998, Intel brought out its follow-up to  the Pentium Pro: The powerful Pentium II Xeon.   Intel designed this chip to tackle the mid-range  workstation and server markets with faster clock   speeds and a large 512-kilobyte L2 cache that  made it more suitable for server platforms. A few months later in March 1999, Intel  released the Pentium III Xeon - a fast,   cheap CPU for web and e-commerce transactions.  While the speed boost over Pentium II Xeon was   small, the successor did feature support for  8-way systems via something called Profusion. This means vendors can build servers with  eight symmetrical processors - essentially   gluing eight CPUs together inside  one box. This broke through a prior   4-way system ceiling that was then causing  performance issues in existing data centers. To note, this 4-way and 8-way systems  feature did require the OS to support   it. This was something that Windows NT/2000  can do, and Linux then had issues with. High end UNIX servers still  retained key advantages. Namely,   certain software like large-scale  databases, data warehouses and CAD   systems required far more main memory than  what x86's 32-bit architecture can allow. But thanks to this pair of Pentiums,   the low to middle ground of UNIX servers  found its flanks open to massive competition. ## The Web Scales Out Sun initially welcomed the Linux revolution. It  was in line with their motto of being "open". So they ported their Java Development Kit  to Linux, and released a Linux port of   workstation hardware. The general  impression they gave was that Sun   doesn't care whether a box runs Linux or  Solaris - it just has to be a SPARC box. But that turned out to be a problem. It didn't  have to be a SPARC box. Serving websites,   email hosting, firewall and other stuff are  not like running DB or analytics software. Companies realized that scaling out  with nodes of Intel silicon running   Linux made more financial sense than  scaling up a big honking UNIX server. This trend suddenly accelerated after the  Dotcom stock bubble exploded. Venture money   dried up and startups started dying. With  frugality the word of the day, companies   saved money by buying second-hand equipment  bought from liquidated failures or Linux. Amazon did a major Linux transition in 2001,   mentioning in their quarterly SEC filing  that it cut their costs by an estimated   $17 million per quarter. When asked about  what they did, an Amazon spokesman said: > "We've always been pretty closed-mouthed about  technology on the back-end stuff, partly because   it's pretty steep tuition and we don't want  other people going to school on our tuition" The online broker Etrade published a fascinating  2006 case study. It compared a Sun 4500 Enterprise   Server that costs $250,000 and can serve about 300  to 400 users to a Linux-Intel box that costs just   $4,000 but serves only 180 people.  How to fix the gap? Get two boxes. Starting in 2001, Linux boxes with Intel silicon  got good enough to steadily replace Sun's in   everything from airline fare to commodities  contracts trading to financial calculations. Sun tried their own scale-out web play with  the Netra. The 2001 Netra X1 model cost as   little as $1,000, but commodity x86 still  provided better performance for the dollar.   The company never really formulated a proper   response to this transition from  Solaris on SPARC to Linux on Intel. ## Going Upscale After winning the low-end game, Linux  now turned its sights to scaling up. In late 2000, IBM's CEO Lou Gerstner  - believing that Linux will change the   world in the same way as the Internet  - announced a massive Linux effort,   investing $1 billion and  dedicating 1,500 employees. January 2001 saw the release of Linux  2.4. Red Hat quickly adopted it for a   subsequent release. It arrived a year  late, but Linux 2.4 delivered the goods   in terms of closing some major performance  gaps with high-end UNIX servers and NT. A major flashpoint during the 1999  Mindcraft tests a few years prior   involved Linux's support of multiprocessor  boxes. That test - confirmed in subsequent   tests - showed that Linux 2.2 did not scale  very well beyond two CPUs in a single system. Windows NT 4.0 and 2000 if  you recall did have that 4,   8, and even 32-way processor support.  So not having it was a major weakness. So Torvalds and company rolled up  their sleeves and worked on it. 2.4   addressed issues like spin locks - allowing  Linux to use 16 or even 32 processors with some   effectiveness. Though I’m not sure how well  it actually ran with that high of a number. It didn't make Linux a challenger to  high end UNIX machines overnight. But   the ability to capably support at least 4  or 8 CPUs cleared a path for Linux on Intel,   or Lintel, to surge into the  middle ground of compute tasks. The economics of Lintel suddenly got  very compelling. A Dell server with   four Xeons running Red Hat Linux at $24,000 costs   half as much as a comparable Sun Fire  UNIX box but performs just as well. Red Hat and IBM immediately began targeting  Sun's Solaris customer base. Hewlett-Packard   and SGI started offering their customers  running proprietary hardware the option to   move to a Linux solution - reasoning that it is  better to maintain that customer relationship. 2002 was a hard year for the server  market, but Linux boxes still grew   swimmingly at the expense of RISC based  systems. Gartner reported that in 2002,   Linux server hardware revenue grew 63%  while UNIX revenue hardware fell 11%. UNIX hardware was still larger revenue-wise  - $17 billion in 2002 compared to Linux's $2   billion - just because these are high end  machines that cost more. But the pressure   was there. By 2004, the average selling price of a  Sun server had fallen 31% from $22,920 to $15,860. ## Opteron and x86-64 One major effort that Intel wanted  for Linux early on was 64-bit support,   meaning for IA-64 or Itanium. In April 1999, Intel spun up Project Trillian, a  consortium of companies that would confidentially   receive Itanium prototypes so they can  develop a Linux port. And in February 2000,   the project released the IA-64 Linux  source code early to the community. Trillian was a milestone in open source  software development history. That being said,   Itanium didn't end up replacing  the 32-bit version of x86, though   HP did adopt it to replace the processors  using their proprietary flavors of UNIX. As we all know, it would be AMD not Intel  that kicked off the 64-bit transition   with their groundbreaking Opteron series of  chips in mid-2003. Some time later in 2004,   Intel released the Nocona Xeon, adopting  AMD's backwards compatible 64-bit extension. 64-bit had been one of the last things  that higher-end UNIX systems still had   over x86. A 32-bit x86 computer addresses  about 4 gigabytes of RAM - far less than   what high end applications like databases or  scientific simulations need to hold in memory. After going 64-bit, an x86 system can now  address dozens or even hundreds of gigabytes of   RAM - removing one of the last major architectural  barriers from switching away from UNIX. Some initially felt that the way Intel  adopted 64-bit was a bit of a kludge or   only a stopgap towards Itanium. Eh,  the results are undeniable. x86-64   bludgeoned the last walls surrounding UNIX.  The Lintel barbarians were now in the castle. ## Windows Then in late 2003, you had the release of Linux  2.6 - which turned out to be a very iconic kernel. Everything about it was improved - speed,  networking, support for up to 64 processors,   and more. You might consider it the  first "enterprise-ready" Linux kernel. Moreover, it arrived just as users of the  now-antiquated Windows NT 4.0 began their   upgrade cycles. They were single and  ready to mingle. IBM, Hewlett-Packard,   Dell and the other sirens sang their  lungs out to woo customers to Linux. IBM in particular led the charge -  training thousands of people in Linux,   helping developers rewrite their  apps for Linux and providing massive   marketing dollars and discounted  machines to potential switchers. How do you fight something that anyone can  download for free?Microsoft's general pitch   was that everyone is already using Office,  so it would be expensive and troublesome   to switch to Linux than it would be  to just buy Windows Server licenses. In 2004, Microsoft ran a "Get the facts"  marketing campaign sharing research purporting   to show Windows in a better light compared  to Linux. The website collected controversy   as those studies were accused as not being  very "impartial" and potentially misleading. A method that I think worked far better  was the deep lock-in afforded by a product   called Active Directory - which Ben  Thompson of Stratechery has since   called "one of the most valuable free  products of all time". What is that? Released as part of Windows 2000,  Active Directory authenticates and   authorizes all the users and assets inside  a Windows network. It lets you push updates,   assign security rights to groups per the  org chart, and validates authentication. So with AD, an administrator can onboard a  new manager, verify their credentials and   give them access to the right tools. And users  can log in to various things with one set of   credentials. It turns a bunch of random Windows  machines into a single manage-able organization. As Ben points out, it also gave  Microsoft ownership of individual   identity. And since identity reached  so deeply into the organization,   it raised the cost of switching to a  level far beyond "just" an OS swap. So in defiance of the people predicting  that Linux would take down Microsoft,   Windows Server sales kept growing. In 2005,   Windows matched UNIX revenue for the first time  ever. The next year, they would surpass it. Linux kept growing, but that growth was  less from eating Windows and more from   eating UNIX or growing in brand new markets where  Windows never got a foothold - supercomputing,   high performance compute,  web, and in the 2010s, cloud. ## Conclusion UNIX server sales would slowly decline in the following years. But it  has not completely died out! Even today, there remain some  customers on Solaris, HP-UX or AIX.   Many such laggard applications  - usually centered in banking or   healthcare - are for one reason or another  too challenging or risky to port to Linux. So why did UNIX lose? I might propose  that it had less to do with technology   than business model. These vertically  integrated kingdoms worked fine years   ago until Intel arrived with  its high volume economics. First, it was Windows NT who hit UNIX hard.  But Linux would go at them even harder - being   able to offer customers everything that UNIX had  without the lock-in. Once Linux got good enough,   the UNIX vendors had no choice  but to make the switch themselves.

transcript_segments.text: Going into the 1990s,
running a big beefy enterprise server  meant UNIX software on RISC hardware.
Then came Intel. And upon its silicon horse rode  two powerful operating systems. One was Windows,
which everyone first thought would win the market.
But then came this new, fast-moving thing
written with the contributions of  thousands around the world. Linux.
In today's video, one of the most fascinating  industrial transitions in computer history:
How Intel, Microsoft and Linux  came together to take down UNIX.
## Beginnings
It is the 1990s and Chipzilla is  seeking new worlds to conquer.
They had won the consumer PC  world by masterfully leveraging
the PC's massive sales volumes. High  volume improves semiconductor yield.
Better yield reduces costs, raises profits,  and throws off more cash to invest back into
better manufacturing. Intel grabbed a lead that  competitors like AMD and Cyrix cannot overcome.
Intel believed that it can run the same playbook  in the world of enterprise servers. Such servers
are used by corporate clients to manage  and serve multiple “client” computers.
Sometimes, people group servers together  with workstations - which are more powerful
desktop computers for intense tasks like  graphics or scientific applications. Such
workstations can also serve a file or two  over a LAN - acting as a low-end server.
On the high end, there are big monolith  computers powered by many CPUs with support
for 64-bit and virtual machine as well as lots  of memory. They run databases, file storage,
and complex business applications -  providing beefy compute via network.
They can also serve websites - which  later became a massive market as the
Internet craze expanded. Though you  don't need a high end machine for that.
## Vertically Integrated At the start of the decade,
this enterprise server market was dominated  by vertically-integrated system vendors.
Such vendors offered a closed, proprietary  system often based on RISC CPUs running a
variant of the UNIX operating system.  The largest and most famous vendor
was Sun Microsystem - which offered their  SPARC chips and Solaris operating system.
Others included IBM with their POWER RISC  chips running the AIX operating system.
And Hewlett-Packard, with their  PA-RISC chips running the HP-UX
operating system. Silicon Graphics as well.
These systems were expensive - running into the  hundreds of thousands of dollars. What's more,
their proprietary nature made switching  nigh impossible. Buy in, get locked in.
## Windows NT
But if Intel wanted to enter the server  market, it needed a strong software partner.
And where did this bring them? To  Microsoft ... and Windows NT. Released
in 1993 by a team led by the legendary  Dave Cutler, NT is a proprietary OS for
both workstations and servers separate  from the consumer-oriented Windows.
While Windows NT Server looks similar  to the consumer product and can run
the same applications, they were  quite different beneath the hood.
Regular Windows is a graphical shell grotesquely  grafted on top of the MS-DOS operating system.
It is said to be possible to clip through  into the horrors of the Backrooms beyond.
NT on the other hand was written from the  ground up for the enterprise. Microsoft
marketed it as being more powerful,  reliable, and with enhanced security.
The first version of NT Server ran on  the Intel 386. It worked fine but it
didn't exactly set the world ablaze. NT was  immature, missing features and capabilities
that its competitors - like IBM's OS/2,  Novell's NetWare and the UNIX variants - had.
And it required rather powerful hardware  (for the time): 16 megabytes of RAM. In 1993,
NT Server sold about 30,000 units  - undoubtedly a disappointment.
But Microsoft is like the Terminator or sequels  to Air Bud: They just keep on coming. Redmond
stayed in the market - adding new features  and sending the UNIX vendors scrambling.
In 1994, Microsoft sold about  115,000 NT licenses. An improvement,
though sales still lagged that of even its  Workstation sibling. But they were growing.
## Pentium Pro
In late 1995, Intel presented  the first chip they really felt
could take them to the server  space: the 32-bit Pentium Pro.
I mentioned the Pentium Pro before.
It had 5.5 million transistors and ran  at about 150-200 megahertz - a great
leap over the original Pentium's 3.1  million transistors and 60 megahertz.
The Pentium Pro slightly outperformed the fastest
RISC chips in certain integer benchmarks.  Which took the community by surprise.
While faster RISC chips like the MIPS R10000  quickly matched afterwards, the Pro reset
the perceived performance limits of what was  previously deemed a mere "desktop" architecture.
The Pentium Pro thusly gave Intel the performance  wedge it needed to invade the server world.
Vendors found that it together with the next  major version of Windows NT - version 4.0,
released earlier that same year - produced  a ready-made server standard that can
match the performance of some RISC-based  integrated systems at a far lower price.
In mid-1995 Intel started circulating example  boards of what they called "Standard High Volume
Servers". These are basic reference models that  partners can adopt to accelerate time-to-market.
The first generation boards  can support 1-4 Pentium Pros,
1-2 gigabytes of working memory, and  hundreds of gigabytes of storage. Intel
said that these servers can handle  up to 2,000 transactions per second.
During the release presentation in  November, Intel announced Pentium
Pro-powered computers ranging from a  $2,600 workstation to a $20,000 server.
In 1996, sales of Windows NT 4.0  grew by 85% - reaching 27% market
share according to IDC. The  competition remained strong,
but Wintel was building up a strong base in  servers, like what they have done in consumer.
## Border Skirmishes
However, Intel knew there were risks in  chaining its enterprise future to Microsoft.
While on the whole Microsoft and Intel  cooperated to grow the PC ecosystem,
breakouts still happened. Most infamously, in  1995 Intel introduced a multimedia software
standard they called "native  signal processing" or NSP.
NSP was Intel’s effort to offload some  demanding audio and video compute to the
CPU via software and APIs. Their thinking was  simple: Get people to buy faster processors.
But Microsoft saw NSP as a "middleware" that  bypassed the OS and so stepped into Windows’ turf.
Microsoft executives made it extremely clear to  Intel that they had issues and publicly announced
that they will not support it. CEO Bill Gates sent  an email to Andy Grove to express his irritation.
The NSP Affair was not the only border  skirmish to occur during this time,
but it is the most well known. Mostly  because it came out during Microsoft's
anti-trust lawsuit as an example  of its anti-competitive behavior.
And when it came out, the  two parties pooh-poohed it,
emphasizing that everything was alright.  But NSP reminded Intel that their partner
was more than willing to exercise its  leverage to kill things it didn’t like.
Unlike the consumer versions of Windows, Windows  NT was built from the ground-up to be portable.
While most instances of NT ran on x86, it also  works on other hardwares like DEC's Alpha CPU,
IBM and Apple's PowerPC, and the RISC design MIPS.
Microsoft continued to seal more chip  support deals - skillfully flanking
Intel right in front of it. A thought  emerged. If NT corners the market,
can Microsoft turn x86 and Intel into just  another hardware architecture amongst many?
## Mismatches
Even if that does not happen, there  still remained the performance issues.
With Moore's Law, Intel gets a new,  faster, better chip every two years.
But Microsoft puts out a new Windows  roughly every three to five years.
And that Windows doesn't always use  everything that Intel's chips had to offer.
Most infamously, Intel first released a  32-bit chip in 1985 - the 386 processor.
Microsoft didn't bring out a 32-bit  consumer OS until 1995 - Windows 95,
in case you were wondering. Ten years later!
Another one occurred during the  Pentium Pro development process,
recounted by Bob Colwell in his  book the Pentium Chronicles.
Microsoft told Intel in many meetings that  Windows 95 (then known as "Chicago") was
going to be 32-bit only with all the  legacy 16-bit code to be removed. This
gave Intel the assurance to optimize  Pentium Pro for 32-bit performance.
So imagine how much constructive confrontation was  forthcoming when Microsoft publicly announced in
1994 that Chicago's graphics display interface  - a key piece of the OS - will remain 16-bits.
It was too late in the development cycle  for Intel to change the Pentium Pro,
so the show went on. And then when it came out,  Intel got dinged in the press for the chip’s
subpar graphics performance on consumer  desktops. Fortunately not a dealbreaker.
And specifically regarding NT and the  server world, Intel felt that NT 4.0's
limits of 4-8 processors per OS instance  imposed a performance ceiling that kept it
out of the high end. To compare, some UNIX  variants can handle up to 64 processors.
This mismatch ties back to the two’s different  growth models, Intel's growth depends on them
selling people the newest chip. So  they want software that helps do that.
Microsoft on the other hand prioritizes  servicing their whole install base. So
they are going to take it slow - emphasizing  backwards compatibility and the whole ecosystem.
And it is not like they don't invest -  developing a new Windows involves thousands
of employees and might cost billions  of dollars. It's just how software is.
So Intel and Microsoft suffer that tension.  But what choice does Intel have with regards to
alternatives? In the late 1990s, one very strong  new candidate appeared on their radar: Linux.
# Stallman
In January 1984, a programmer at MIT named Richard  Stallman formally began a project to replace UNIX.
Stallman hailed from the MIT AI Lab,
which appeared in my video about Lisp  machines, AI, and expert systems.
Lisp began as an elegant research  tool for early AI research. But when
businesspeople recognized that Lisp and  the AI it powers can be a big industry,
the Lab split apart into two companies,  Symbolics and Lisp Machines Inc.
Symbolics raised millions to try and  become the Nvidia of its day - hiring
away the Lab's top hackers and leaving it a  shell of itself. Stallman never forgave this.
"Everything's dying" he would later say.
Motivated by deep feelings of  loss over his hacker community,
he decided to start a new one - founded  on top of the concept of free software.
Thusly in late 1983, he embarked on  a project to build a free operating
system that followed UNIX's design  principles - like its modularity and
portability across hardware - without  copying it for trade secret reasons.
The thing was called GNU - which he said  to mean "GNU's Not UNIX". Stallman didn't
know if he would ever finish it, but with such  things you will never know if you don’t start.
Over the next few years, Stallman and his new  community built out the various bits of the
toolchain. But there was one thing missing:  The kernel, which suffered incessant delays.
This was a pretty major piece. The  kernel bridges the OS and the hardware.
It manages memory, how much CPU  time a process gets, disk space,
and more. Even the name sounds important. It sits  at the very heart of the whole operating system.
## Linus and Linux
That kernel finally arrived thanks to the  work of a 21-year old Finnish undergraduate
named Linus Torvalds, who was inspired by  an educational UNIX-based OS called MINIX.
Very famous story. You probably  heard it before. In August 1991,
he posted on the MINIX Usenet group that he was  making a free hobbyist OS and requested feature
ideas. It drew contributors from that ecosystem  and eventually spun off into its own: Linux.
Linus's role in the Linux project soon changes  from coder to that of a leader who reviews
other people’s contributions and merges them  into the code base. This approach - famously
described as like a bazaar - lets Linux  ship new code faster than companies can.
The first workable version of Linux  released in October 1991. Then in 1992,
version 0.12 adopted Stallman's license, GPL.  This allowed anyone to read and modify Linux’s
code so long as those modifications  are also open sourced, if distributed.
So GPL prevented companies from taking the code,
adding some salt on top and re-selling  the result as a competing closed-source
product - thereby saving the Linux kernel from  the same fragmentation issues that afflicted UNIX.
It also assured companies that any work they did  to improve the kernel would help everyone and not
get locked away. Companies as large as IBM would  have hundreds of their employees contributing
code. Torvalds would later famously say that  going GPL was the best thing that he ever did.
## Distros and Red Hat
The GPL also made possible the  business of commercial distribution.
Linux is a kernel - a car engine. Very important,
but you still kinda need the rest of the  car. That might be fine for early adopters,
it is not practical to ask ordinary users  to build their car before driving it.
So people started doing distributions  or "distros". Distributions package the
Linux kernel along with utilities from  the GNU Project or other free software
to produce an OS bundle that is  slightly more convenient to use.
It is like those mixtapes we senior citizens  used to pass around to each other in high school.
Good distros became popular enough to  monetize. Someone likened the business
model to selling bottled water. Different  packaging, same water ... unless you are
a Nongfu Water extremist and really into  the "natural over purified" water thing.
Anyway. Notable early distributions of this  GNU/Linux operating system - which I must shorten
to Linux for the sake of brevity but let us not  forget GNU - include Slackware and Debian ...
and Red Hat, which was first set up by  Marc Ewing in 1993. Ewing adopted Linux early,
but after some time realized that he was  spending more time managing his Linux
box than actually developing  software. I know the feeling.
So he made a distribution called Red Hat in  the spare bedroom of his apartment near Duke
University. Named to memorialize a red  and white striped lacrosse cap he used
to wear in college. Though the logo looks  more like a fedora or a trilby, M’lady.
Red Hat provided things around Linux  to make it a more professional product.
Like for example, the Red Hat Package  Manager utility, which helps users add,
remove, or update software packages  that do stuff like Web or FTP.
The Red Hat distribution can then be put  on a CD and sold in retail shops. In 1995,
Marc Ewing and colleague Robert Young founded Red  Hat the company, which earned revenue from selling
those CDs as well as accompanying training,  education and customer support services.
In its first years, Linux was something  for highly technical hackers and broke
college students. The rise of Red Hat  and other commercial distributions like
Caldera helped usher Linux out of that early  space and into the corporate mainstream.
## An OS With Opportunity
Linux adoption started small  but grew fast. By mid-1997,
its worldwide user base was conservatively  estimated at around 3-5 million.
Yeah sure that far lags Windows' 100  million users and Apple Macintosh’s 50+
million. But in early 1992, Linux had maybe a  few hundred users. And 1996, maybe 1-2 million.
What was driving all this uptake? It was more  than just price, though price of course played
a factor. A Red Hat disc and box retailed  at about $50. Windows NT licenses on the
other hand might sell for anywhere from $150  for a single upgrade to $1100 for a 10-seat
package. And UNIX systems with hardware and  software will cost $25,000 to $250,000 or more.
Byte Magazine ran a story in 1997  mentioning a systems consultant for
Eastman Kodak installing Linux to aid in  some project for their Photo CD product,
and saving the company $10,000 by not  getting a high-priced UNIX alternative.
Considering how the Photo CD  ended up, good savings indeed.
But interestingly, companies and organizations  did not adopt Linux just because it was cheap.
A significant Linux advantage was  its reliability. One user said that
it was almost "crash-proof", which  translates to better productivity.
And for sophisticated users, they loved that  they can access its source code - something
Microsoft would never let anyone do with  Windows. So people can customize their
Linux to do things on the fly. People  tweaked Linux to run on a Palm Pilot.
Researchers at Los Alamos used Linux to network  together 68 PCs to simulate atomic shock waves.
On the other hand, it was true that Linux also  had glaring shortcomings. First and foremost,
it had nowhere near as many applications  as Windows or Mac. There was no good Linux
version of Microsoft Office, Visual  Basic, or other business software.
I like how Byte said all that, then added right  afterwards that Linux did include lots of tools
that you can use to create your own applications.  That is the kind of audience, I reckon.
Another issue is getting  support. If something goes wrong,
what documentation can you consult. And  who can you call? Though that is where
companies like Red Hat and Caldera  can step in, providing tech support.
One last issue about Linux was its reputation.  Despite not sharing a direct lineage, it is
often associated with UNIX - which means receiving  UNIX's aura of being inscrutable and hard to use.
And despite the fast growth, all  the prestigious names adopting it,
and the real price-performance benefits, there  still remained a negative bias amongst company
executives. A manager might often ask "How can  you possibly consider it for a critical server?"
Yet even as they ask that, Linux probably was  already running somewhere in their company.
One anonymous system administrator  told the SF Chronicle in 1998:
> "Many management types distrust Linux because  it is free. But they put me in charge of running
their servers and I am going to use what  works best. What works best is Linux".
## Meet Intel
In early 1998, Intel started receiving these  strange requests from across the country.
Engineers and researchers at places like US's
Fermi National Lab were asking Intel  to port its math libraries to Linux.
Prior to this, Intel had minimal involvement  with Linux - maybe fixing a bug or two.
However, checks with OEMs making white-label  computer servers for customers like small
Internet Service Providers showed them  that Linux growth was exploding upwards.
Almost 20% of public web servers ran it - an  unexpectedly high market share considering
that the OS had little to no presence on  the desktop. Still doesn't, by the way.
This news went straight up to Andy Grove,  who remarked in rather colorful language
that they should be doing something about  this. So Intel executives reached out to
Red Hat and in a series of meetings, tried  to learn about how this company worked.
And it sort of baffled them. Red Hat doesn't  own the underlying IP behind its core software
product, which anyone can get for free. How  does that make money? How’s this investable?
But the guys at Red Hat kept talking. CEO  Robert Young liked to use this ketchup metaphor:
Anyone with tomatoes, sugar and vinegar can make  ketchup, yet Heinz owns 80% of that market. And
Linux advocates inside Intel shared data points  of what they learned on ISP adoption. In the end,
Intel management was convinced and the two  companies started talking about partnerships.
As I mentioned earlier, Intel increasingly felt  that it would be risky to rely on just Windows NT.
They were working on a new chip called "Merced",  the first implementation of their 64-bit IA-64
server architecture. It shall later be branded  as Itanium, and was said to be blazingly fast.
But worries lingered that NT would  shackle its full power - same as how
things went with 32-bit for literally a  decade. Perhaps reinforcing those fears,
Microsoft's next version of NT -  then called NT 5.0 - was delayed
from 1998 to 1999. After yet further delays,  Microsoft renamed NT 5.0 to Windows 2000.
Now Intel can support and contribute to Linux  development - tuning it to take advantage
of Intel's latest and greatest silicon - and  make it a compelling alternative to Windows.
## Summer of Linux
The summer of 1998 saw multiple big  companies making Linux announcements.
In June 1998, IBM - one of the most  conservative companies out there - said
that it will include an open source web  server software called Apache in its suite
of e-commerce tools. Apache isn't Linux,  but most Apache server instances run on it.
IBM first encountered Apache back in 1996  when they selected it for the website of
the Atlanta Summer Olympics. Now they  were giving it their stamp of approval,
officially giving open source its  first foothold into the enterprise.
Another famous adopter was  Oracle. On July 6th 1998,
InfoWorld published an article titled  "Linux not yet critical mass". In it,
Oracle - plus Sybase and Informix - said  they had no intentions of releasing their
DB software for Linux. A rep said they weren’t  seeing a big demand from customers for it.
Three days later, Oracle announced  that they were porting their Oracle8
database to Linux. A major reason  for this abrupt turnaround was a
panel discussion held at Santa Clara in  July 1998 called "the Future of Linux".
Over 900 or so people came to see Torvalds  and others. In the panel, they discussed
whether open source was a fad, urged users to push  application vendors to port to Linux, and more.
People later identify that panel as a major  turning point. By September 1998, several large
companies had Linux ports including the enterprise  systems company Computer Associates, software
maker Corel, and database company Informix. The  trend would continue in the subsequent years.
## Intel and Red Hat
Intel was also at that July  "Future of Linux" panel.
Intel's Sunil Saxena gave a presentation  saying that Linux was becoming the OS of
choice for Internet Service Providers while  also noting some of its weaknesses - like
scalability, drivers for high end  hardware, and large memory support.
He emphasized that Intel wanted to support  Linux. And those words were soon backed with
action on September 29th when Intel announced  that it - along with the web browser company
Netscape and VC firms Benchmark and  Greylock - would invest in Red Hat.
Now, Intel was saying they wanted Intel  silicon to run Linux as well as it did
Windows NT and everything else. They  will work with Red Hat - providing
technical contribution plus a dedicated Intel  engineering liaison for the Linux community.
Cherry on top, Intel also said they  will join Linux International - an
early worldwide Linux advocacy organization.
After the announcement, another  critical but underrated domino falls.
One Benchmark partner was also a board  member at Dell, and through him Red Hat
got in front of Michael Dell. They started  talking about Linux's growth on the server,
how the market might shape up, and  if Linux can ever win the desktop.
Dell eventually invested into Red Hat. And  more importantly, they later announce in
early 1999 that they will start preinstalling  Linux on workstations and servers - the first
major vendor to do this. Suddenly Linux is  on the same pedestal as Windows and Novell.
## Microsoft
When news of Intel's Red Hat investment  came out, the tech media went into a
frenzy speculating what this might mean  for the Intel-Microsoft relationship.
Red Hat's executives recounted in  the book "Under the Radar" that
Microsoft "went ballistic" after Intel  announced their investment. That weekend,
Intel executives took multiple angry  calls from their Microsoft counterparts.
Prior to 1998, Microsoft maybe could have nixed  the Intel investment. But in May that year,
the US government charged Microsoft  for monopolistic actions - particularly
regarding how it bundled Internet Explorer  with Windows during the Browser Wars.
The trial and scrutiny meant that Microsoft had to
temper its behavior. Publicly they  issued a statement citing Red Hat as
evidence that Microsoft didn't actually  have a monopoly on operating systems.
Interestingly, Microsoft would later  invoke Linux as evidence that there
remained enough competition in the OS market  that the government shouldn't break them up.
But internally, they were  concerned. In October 1998,
a set of Microsoft memos - infamously  named the Halloween Memos - leaked,
called the rise of free software like Linux  a long-term credible threat to Windows.
They then reportedly formed a "Linux  attack team" to convince customers
that it was not ready. They posted  a web page called "Linux Myths",
that tries to "step back from the  hype and look at the reality".
It then addresses various "myths" chanted  by the Linux faithful like "Linux performs
better than Windows NT 4", and "Linux is more  reliable than Windows NT 4" and "Linux is free".
Infamously in April 1999, Microsoft  sponsored benchmark tests by a third
party lab called Mindcraft that  showed NT outperforming Linux
as a file server by 2.5 times  and web server by 3.7 times.
## Port of Choice
Intel dodged Gates’ fury by  declaring that it was OS neutral.
So Linux, Novell’s Netware, Sun’s  Solaris and Microsoft’s Windows 2000,
Intel wanted all of them to  run well on its hardware.
Intel (along with twenty other companies)  even tried to unite the thirty or so UNIX
variants out there using a thing  called Uniform Driver Initiative
so that vendors can write drivers for  Intel hardware. It didn't end up so well.
Later in 2010, Intel would formalize this  Switzerland strategy as "Port of Choice",
but CTO Pat Gelsinger called it a long-standing  strategy in 2001. And in the end, the OS
makers had to accept it, because Intel  silicon then had no real alternatives.
In mid-1998, Intel brought out its follow-up to  the Pentium Pro: The powerful Pentium II Xeon.
Intel designed this chip to tackle the mid-range  workstation and server markets with faster clock
speeds and a large 512-kilobyte L2 cache that  made it more suitable for server platforms.
A few months later in March 1999, Intel  released the Pentium III Xeon - a fast,
cheap CPU for web and e-commerce transactions.  While the speed boost over Pentium II Xeon was
small, the successor did feature support for  8-way systems via something called Profusion.
This means vendors can build servers with  eight symmetrical processors - essentially
gluing eight CPUs together inside  one box. This broke through a prior
4-way system ceiling that was then causing  performance issues in existing data centers.
To note, this 4-way and 8-way systems  feature did require the OS to support
it. This was something that Windows NT/2000  can do, and Linux then had issues with.
High end UNIX servers still  retained key advantages. Namely,
certain software like large-scale  databases, data warehouses and CAD
systems required far more main memory than  what x86's 32-bit architecture can allow.
But thanks to this pair of Pentiums,
the low to middle ground of UNIX servers  found its flanks open to massive competition.
## The Web Scales Out
Sun initially welcomed the Linux revolution. It  was in line with their motto of being "open".
So they ported their Java Development Kit  to Linux, and released a Linux port of
workstation hardware. The general  impression they gave was that Sun
doesn't care whether a box runs Linux or  Solaris - it just has to be a SPARC box.
But that turned out to be a problem. It didn't  have to be a SPARC box. Serving websites,
email hosting, firewall and other stuff are  not like running DB or analytics software.
Companies realized that scaling out  with nodes of Intel silicon running
Linux made more financial sense than  scaling up a big honking UNIX server.
This trend suddenly accelerated after the  Dotcom stock bubble exploded. Venture money
dried up and startups started dying. With  frugality the word of the day, companies
saved money by buying second-hand equipment  bought from liquidated failures or Linux.
Amazon did a major Linux transition in 2001,
mentioning in their quarterly SEC filing  that it cut their costs by an estimated
$17 million per quarter. When asked about  what they did, an Amazon spokesman said:
> "We've always been pretty closed-mouthed about  technology on the back-end stuff, partly because
it's pretty steep tuition and we don't want  other people going to school on our tuition"
The online broker Etrade published a fascinating  2006 case study. It compared a Sun 4500 Enterprise
Server that costs $250,000 and can serve about 300  to 400 users to a Linux-Intel box that costs just
$4,000 but serves only 180 people.  How to fix the gap? Get two boxes.
Starting in 2001, Linux boxes with Intel silicon  got good enough to steadily replace Sun's in
everything from airline fare to commodities  contracts trading to financial calculations.
Sun tried their own scale-out web play with  the Netra. The 2001 Netra X1 model cost as
little as $1,000, but commodity x86 still  provided better performance for the dollar.
The company never really formulated a proper
response to this transition from  Solaris on SPARC to Linux on Intel.
## Going Upscale
After winning the low-end game, Linux  now turned its sights to scaling up.
In late 2000, IBM's CEO Lou Gerstner  - believing that Linux will change the
world in the same way as the Internet  - announced a massive Linux effort,
investing $1 billion and  dedicating 1,500 employees.
January 2001 saw the release of Linux  2.4. Red Hat quickly adopted it for a
subsequent release. It arrived a year  late, but Linux 2.4 delivered the goods
in terms of closing some major performance  gaps with high-end UNIX servers and NT.
A major flashpoint during the 1999  Mindcraft tests a few years prior
involved Linux's support of multiprocessor  boxes. That test - confirmed in subsequent
tests - showed that Linux 2.2 did not scale  very well beyond two CPUs in a single system.
Windows NT 4.0 and 2000 if  you recall did have that 4,
8, and even 32-way processor support.  So not having it was a major weakness.
So Torvalds and company rolled up  their sleeves and worked on it. 2.4
addressed issues like spin locks - allowing  Linux to use 16 or even 32 processors with some
effectiveness. Though I’m not sure how well  it actually ran with that high of a number.
It didn't make Linux a challenger to  high end UNIX machines overnight. But
the ability to capably support at least 4  or 8 CPUs cleared a path for Linux on Intel,
or Lintel, to surge into the  middle ground of compute tasks.
The economics of Lintel suddenly got  very compelling. A Dell server with
four Xeons running Red Hat Linux at $24,000 costs
half as much as a comparable Sun Fire  UNIX box but performs just as well.
Red Hat and IBM immediately began targeting  Sun's Solaris customer base. Hewlett-Packard
and SGI started offering their customers  running proprietary hardware the option to
move to a Linux solution - reasoning that it is  better to maintain that customer relationship.
2002 was a hard year for the server  market, but Linux boxes still grew
swimmingly at the expense of RISC based  systems. Gartner reported that in 2002,
Linux server hardware revenue grew 63%  while UNIX revenue hardware fell 11%.
UNIX hardware was still larger revenue-wise  - $17 billion in 2002 compared to Linux's $2
billion - just because these are high end  machines that cost more. But the pressure
was there. By 2004, the average selling price of a  Sun server had fallen 31% from $22,920 to $15,860.
## Opteron and x86-64
One major effort that Intel wanted  for Linux early on was 64-bit support,
meaning for IA-64 or Itanium.
In April 1999, Intel spun up Project Trillian, a  consortium of companies that would confidentially
receive Itanium prototypes so they can  develop a Linux port. And in February 2000,
the project released the IA-64 Linux  source code early to the community.
Trillian was a milestone in open source  software development history. That being said,
Itanium didn't end up replacing  the 32-bit version of x86, though
HP did adopt it to replace the processors  using their proprietary flavors of UNIX.
As we all know, it would be AMD not Intel  that kicked off the 64-bit transition
with their groundbreaking Opteron series of  chips in mid-2003. Some time later in 2004,
Intel released the Nocona Xeon, adopting  AMD's backwards compatible 64-bit extension.
64-bit had been one of the last things  that higher-end UNIX systems still had
over x86. A 32-bit x86 computer addresses  about 4 gigabytes of RAM - far less than
what high end applications like databases or  scientific simulations need to hold in memory.
After going 64-bit, an x86 system can now  address dozens or even hundreds of gigabytes of
RAM - removing one of the last major architectural  barriers from switching away from UNIX.
Some initially felt that the way Intel  adopted 64-bit was a bit of a kludge or
only a stopgap towards Itanium. Eh,  the results are undeniable. x86-64
bludgeoned the last walls surrounding UNIX.  The Lintel barbarians were now in the castle.
## Windows
Then in late 2003, you had the release of Linux  2.6 - which turned out to be a very iconic kernel.
Everything about it was improved - speed,  networking, support for up to 64 processors,
and more. You might consider it the  first "enterprise-ready" Linux kernel.
Moreover, it arrived just as users of the  now-antiquated Windows NT 4.0 began their
upgrade cycles. They were single and  ready to mingle. IBM, Hewlett-Packard,
Dell and the other sirens sang their  lungs out to woo customers to Linux.
IBM in particular led the charge -  training thousands of people in Linux,
helping developers rewrite their  apps for Linux and providing massive
marketing dollars and discounted  machines to potential switchers.
How do you fight something that anyone can  download for free?Microsoft's general pitch
was that everyone is already using Office,  so it would be expensive and troublesome
to switch to Linux than it would be  to just buy Windows Server licenses.
In 2004, Microsoft ran a "Get the facts"  marketing campaign sharing research purporting
to show Windows in a better light compared  to Linux. The website collected controversy
as those studies were accused as not being  very "impartial" and potentially misleading.
A method that I think worked far better  was the deep lock-in afforded by a product
called Active Directory - which Ben  Thompson of Stratechery has since
called "one of the most valuable free  products of all time". What is that?
Released as part of Windows 2000,  Active Directory authenticates and
authorizes all the users and assets inside  a Windows network. It lets you push updates,
assign security rights to groups per the  org chart, and validates authentication.
So with AD, an administrator can onboard a  new manager, verify their credentials and
give them access to the right tools. And users  can log in to various things with one set of
credentials. It turns a bunch of random Windows  machines into a single manage-able organization.
As Ben points out, it also gave  Microsoft ownership of individual
identity. And since identity reached  so deeply into the organization,
it raised the cost of switching to a  level far beyond "just" an OS swap.
So in defiance of the people predicting  that Linux would take down Microsoft,
Windows Server sales kept growing. In 2005,
Windows matched UNIX revenue for the first time  ever. The next year, they would surpass it.
Linux kept growing, but that growth was  less from eating Windows and more from
eating UNIX or growing in brand new markets where  Windows never got a foothold - supercomputing,
high performance compute,  web, and in the 2010s, cloud.
## Conclusion UNIX server sales would slowly decline in
the following years. But it  has not completely died out!
Even today, there remain some  customers on Solaris, HP-UX or AIX.
Many such laggard applications  - usually centered in banking or
healthcare - are for one reason or another  too challenging or risky to port to Linux.
So why did UNIX lose? I might propose  that it had less to do with technology
than business model. These vertically  integrated kingdoms worked fine years
ago until Intel arrived with  its high volume economics.
First, it was Windows NT who hit UNIX hard.  But Linux would go at them even harder - being
able to offer customers everything that UNIX had  without the lock-in. Once Linux got good enough,
the UNIX vendors had no choice  but to make the switch themselves.
